Cool weather, settled championships weigh on Las Vegas F1 ticket demand

Formula One F1 - Las Vegas Grand Prix - Las Vegas Strip Circuit, Las Vegas, Nevada, United States - November 19, 2026 General view of a Las Vegas sign ahead of practice REUTERS/Jeenah Moon

LAS VEGAS, Nov 19 : Ticket prices for Saturday's Las Vegas Grand Prix are on course to be their lowest since Formula One debuted on the Strip in 2023, secondary-market platform TickPick said, as a lack of championship suspense and chilly weather weigh on demand. The average purchase price for Saturday race-day tickets stood at $781, down 12 per cent from $889 last year and 36 per cent below the $1,214 paid for the inaugural event in 2023, according to TickPick. The cheapest available ticket for Saturday's race was $470, while entry to Thursday's practice session was available from $67.  This year's event comes after Mercedes secured both the drivers' and constructors' championships, removing the title implications that can help fuel late-season interest.

A NOVELTY NO MORE The first Las Vegas race drew fans partly because of its novelty, while the 2024 edition saw Red Bull's Max Verstappen clinch a fourth successive drivers' title on the high-speed street circuit. "When the Las Vegas Grand Prix was first introduced in 2023, it generated tons of excitement from F1 fans across the US, and demand was reflected in the $1,214 average purchase price for a ticket that year," said Kyle Zorn, TickPick's director of content. "Now in its fourth year, some of the initial excitement surrounding the Las Vegas Grand Prix has faded, and ticket prices have consistently declined since that first year."  Cold and wet weather added another variable in the buildup, with rain and low temperatures on Thursday ahead of first practice. Conditions are expected to be dry but cool for Friday qualifying and Saturday night's race. "I feel like the destination is buzzing," Emily Prazer, Formula One's chief commercial officer and president and chief executive of the Las Vegas Grand Prix, told reporters on Wednesday. She noted the number of activations across the city had reached an all-time high, and said the challenge for organizers was to improve on the previous year's event. 10-YEAR EXTENSION Formula One signed a 10-year extension in June to keep Las Vegas on the calendar through 2037. The race is unusual in that Formula One itself promotes the event rather than relying on a third-party promoter. "It feels like it's really Formula One's home in North America," Prazer said.  "And expectations are high when you're Formula One putting on the race."  Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli, who this month became Formula One's youngest world champion, said the low temperatures could make the race an "outlier," with tire management likely to play a decisive role. "Having tires in the right temperature is going to be key," said the 20-year-old Italian, who named Red Bull, McLaren and Ferrari as Mercedes' main rivals for the weekend. "Track evolution is going to be massive."

Source: Reuters

CAPE TOWN, Nov 19 : New Zealand and South Africa will look to return to winning ways this weekend as they battle for a place in the Nations Championship final at the end of the month, while France are well placed to reach the decider. The All Blacks and Springboks are the top two teams in World Rugby’s rankings but suffered surprise defeats last weekend, with France edging South Africa 21-19 in Paris on Friday and Wales ending a 73-year wait to overcome New Zealand. South Africa’s preparations have been further disrupted by a six-match suspension imposed on coach Rassie Erasmus by World Rugby after he questioned the integrity of match officials following the defeat at the Stade de France. He will be forced to watch his side’s clash with Ireland on Saturday from his Dublin hotel room, although he has bizarrely organised an online watch party to which 62,000 supporters had signed up by Thursday afternoon.

The four-time World Cup winners’ hopes of reaching the final on November 29 will depend on the outcome of their match against Ireland and New Zealand’s earlier clash with England on a busy Saturday when all 12 competing countries are in action. BONUS-POINT WIN WOULD PUT ALL BLACKS IN FINAL The All Blacks are one point ahead of the Boks in the Southern Hemisphere standings and a bonus-point victory over England at Twickenham will ensure they finish top. Anything less opens the door for South Africa, who will know what they are required to do when they take to the field in Dublin but are expected to be given a torrid time by their hosts. Ireland are in a three-way scramble for top place in the Northern Hemisphere standings, where France sit in pole position. The French have a one-point lead over England and Ireland. The also arguably have an easier assignment at home to Argentina. Saturday’s six matches will determine the final standings in the two sections and the fixtures for finals weekend from November 27-29, when all six games will be played at Twickenham. The only certainty is that Italy will finish last in the Northern Hemisphere standings and contest the 11th-place playoff next Friday. Each team will face the side finishing in the equivalent position in the other hemisphere’s section to determine the final placings. Australia, who have lost their last eight tests in Europe, can still finish third in the Southern Hemisphere standings if they beat Wales in Cardiff and other results go their way. They will, however, have to deal with an ebullient atmosphere after last Saturday’s historic win over the All Blacks. The result provided a massive boost for rugby in Wales, which has been in turmoil in recent times. Coach Steve Tandy insisted there would be no hangover after the Welsh celebrations. “We enjoyed the moment – we didn’t brush over it too quickly. Then we turned the page with the players,” he said on Thursday.

(Editing by Pritha Sarkar)

TOKYO, Nov 20 : Japan's annual core inflation accelerated in October and exceeded the central bank's 2 per cent target for the second straight month, a sign of broadening price pressures that cements the case for a near-term interest rate. The data will be among factors the Bank of Japan will scrutinise at its next two-day policy meeting ending on December 18, when many market players expect the central bank to hike its policy rate to 1.5 per cent from the current 1.25 per cent. The core consumer price index (CPI), which strips away the effect of volatile fresh food, rose 2.2 per cent in October from a year earlier, data showed on Friday, compared with a median market forecast for a 2.3 per cent gain. It followed a 2.1 per cent rise in September. An index that strips away the effects of both volatile fresh food and fuel, which is closely watched by the BOJ as a better gauge of demand-driven price pressures, rose 2.2 per cent in October from a year earlier after increasing 2.4 per cent in September.

Marcel Thieliant, head of Asia-Pacific at Capital Economics, expects inflation, excluding fresh food and energy, to accelerate sharply over the coming months as firms continue to pass on rising raw material costs. "The upshot is that we now expect the Bank of Japan to lift rates to 2.5 per cent by the middle of next year," he wrote in a research note. With stubbornly high energy costs and rising import prices from a weak yen adding to inflationary pressures, the BOJ raised its policy rate to 1.25 per cent in September after delivering a hike in June — a shorter interval than the roughly twice-a-year hikes in 2024 and 2025. The central bank kept rates steady last month, declaring victory in its 14-year battle to hit its price target.

WASHINGTON: The Trump administration is considering requiring US companies to publicly disclose their use of Chinese AI models, a bid to discourage reliance on the technology without imposing new restrictions that could anger industry or Beijing, three people told Reuters. The Treasury Department and the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP) have discussed the plan, which would apply to companies such as Airbnb, the people said. The company uses Qwen, an AI model made by China's Alibaba, to power its AI customer service agent. Under the plan, companies like Airbnb would be required to post that information on their websites. It was not immediately clear if the idea was gaining traction within the administration or if it would be enshrined in a formal rulemaking process if it does move forward.

But its consideration, first reported by Reuters, underscores an emerging push within the administration toward combating the spread of powerful Chinese open weight models, a source of deep concern within the government. Open weight models make their core components publicly available for anyone to download and adapt. The proposal also shows officials are looking at ways to discourage use of Chinese AI through a "name and shame" campaign while sticking to a broader anti-regulation stance on AI. The White House, the Treasury Department and Alibaba did not respond to requests for comment. Airbnb said in a statement that its AI activity "runs overwhelmingly on US-origin models" and the company uses "only a limited number of China-origin models, all of which are open-source and run only through approved US-based service providers, keeping data and operations separate and protected". The Chinese Embassy in Washington said Beijing opposes politicising trade and tech issues, which will "only stifle global AI advances and serve no one's interests. We will resolutely safeguard Chinese businesses' lawful rights and interests", it added. The consideration comes as revelations about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy have fueled renewed calls in Washington for a tougher stance on China . They have turned a spotlight on cases of Nvidia AI chips being smuggled to China that went unpunished, dialing up pressure on the Trump administration to crack down on Chinese tech threats.

Also read:

China's access to Nvidia chips in doubt as curbs gain traction in US Congress

Nvidia faces deepening scrutiny over China chip ties, CEO affair

Chinese-made open-weight models are gaining ground with US companies because they are cheaper than proprietary AI tools from top US labs OpenAI and Anthropic, and perform well enough. But China hawks fear Beijing is using such models - like Moonshot AI's Kimi, DeepSeek or Qwen - to hook US companies so they will become dependent on Chinese AI. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in July that the Trump administration could sanction Chinese AI companies if they were found to be guilty of intellectual property theft via distillation of American models. Distillation is the process of training smaller AI models using the output of larger ones as part of an effort to lower the costs of training a powerful new AI tool. Bessent's remarks echoed comments in April by Michael Kratsios, OSTP director, who accused China of stealing US artificial intelligence labs' intellectual property on an "industrial scale", spurring a State Department-led push to highlight such behavior to foreign counterparts.

Also read:

US to curb China's access to AI chips as Trump heads to Asia

China slams new US chip curbs, vows 'necessary measures'

CONGRESSIONAL INVESTIGATION But US officials have stopped short of restricting or taking punitive action against Chinese AI companies. The issue has attracted the attention of Congress. Republican US Representatives Andrew Garbarino of New York and John Moolenaar of Michigan, who chair the House Homeland Security Committee and the House select committee on China, respectively, launched an investigation into American companies' use of Chinese AI this year. They sent letters to Airbnb as well as Anysphere, the maker of the AI coding tool Cursor, whose Composer 2 AI model was built on a version of Kimi. A letter was also sent to DoorDash, whose co-founder said the company routes some tasks in an internal system through Kimi. Moonshot, DoorDash, and SpaceX, which bought Anysphere, did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Moolenaar welcomed news of the Trump administration's deliberations. "Disclosure is an important step in managing the potential risks posed by the diffusion of Chinese open-weight models in the United States,” he said in a statement to Reuters, noting that risks remain even if U companies run Chinese AI models on their own infrastructure. Canada-based Thomson Reuters, which owns Reuters, also uses Alibaba's Qwen, according to a TR spokesperson. She noted that the model was "substantially retrained" to align "with our standards for safety, accuracy and neutrality", and runs entirely within the company's own infrastructure. Chinese AI models were the three most popular by token usage in October on OpenRouter, an AI marketplace platform that tracks usage data. Tokens are units of data processed by AI models. Chinese AI models have even been used by the US government itself. Reuters reported in September that a US government website deployed an AI model from China's Alibaba to allow users to search proposed federal regulations even though the FBI accused the model's developer of copying Anthropic's technology. American open-weight models include Meta's Muse Glimmer, Nvidia's Nemotron and Reflection AI's Beam.

Source: Reuters/co

FAST

NEW YORK, Nov 19 : The market share battle between the two top US exchanges has never been so lopsided. With Anthropic's record-breaking initial public offering on Wednesday, Nasdaq snatched another marquee listing from the New York Stock Exchange this year, adding to its already wide lead in the battle for market share against its downtown rival. The exchange displayed the Anthropic win on the huge screens that envelop its Times Square address on Thursday, as more than 800 million shares changed hands in the AI company's debut. "Anthropic’s IPO is a very proud moment for us," said Adena Friedman, chief executive officer of Nasdaq, in an interview Thursday. "We’ve been engaging with the Anthropic team for a very long time. Separate from the entire listing experience, we've been a client to them, as we are to the AI ecosystem, and so we also have gotten to know them in that context as well." Over the last decade, the listing advantage has swung decisively in Nasdaq's favor. According to data from Dealogic, there have been 64 IPOs — led by Anthropic and SpaceX — on Nasdaq so far this year, raising about $201.8 billion, dwarfing the $20.8 billion haul raised from 42 IPOs on NYSE.

That is the widest gap in terms of capital raised between the two exchanges record since Dealogic started tracking the data in 1995. In 2017, NYSE raked in share sale proceeds of $28.8 billion from 69 deals, versus Nasdaq's $9.3 billion haul from 86 flotations. However, Nasdaq finished ahead of NYSE six out of eight times between 2018 and 2025, according to Dealogic, and is on track to do so again this year. Nasdaq’s run of dominance can be linked to several moves the exchange operator has made over the years. Friedman, who has led Nasdaq for a decade, on Thursday cited the exchange operator's strength in marketing IPOs, its investor relations business that helps connect companies with large asset managers and institutional investors, and its index business — which it launched in 1985 — as key competitive advantages. These efforts have allowed it to build relationships with founders in big IPO hubs like Silicon Valley and contributed to its dominance in tech listings. "It's a very hard problem (for NYSE) to solve because Nasdaq didn't build its private markets business or its index just two years ago. They have had a head start of several years compared to their competitors. NYSE will have to probably just copy what Nasdaq has done for the past 10 years," said Owen Lau, an analyst at Clear Street. NYSE executives are under increasing pressure to win the next mega-IPO after the recent losses to Nasdaq, according to two people familiar with the matter. The NYSE did not respond to a request for comment. "Probably the major reason (for their dominance) is that Nasdaq has their own indexes," said Lau, referring to the Nasdaq 100 and the Nasdaq Composite, which are licensed for use by institutional asset managers. "That is a very big draw for many companies such as SpaceX and Anthropic." The Nasdaq 100's constituents include several of the world's most valuable companies, such as Apple, Nvidia and Alphabet. STRATEGIC ADVANTAGE Admission to benchmarks like the Nasdaq 100 or S&P 500 gives companies increased access to deep-pocketed institutions with large index funds. This broadens the companies' shareholder base and improves share liquidity. The NYSE has a similar index that tracks its 100 largest US stocks that it launched last year, but it is less widely followed by investors. Nasdaq introduced new rules earlier this year to speed the addition of newly listed megacap companies to the index, a move experts say gives them another advantage over the NYSE, even as it has drawn criticism from some quarters. In an interview with Bloomberg in May, NYSE President Lynn Martin called the rule changes "questionable." On Thursday, Friedman said only a handful of megacap companies of the size and scale of Anthropic and SpaceX have the potential to be fast-tracked into the Nasdaq 100, adding that market liquidity is not an issue. Reuters reported in March that SpaceX made early inclusion in the Nasdaq 100 a necessary condition to list on the Nasdaq. The exchange ultimately added the company to the index 15 days after its stock market debut.

Source: Reuters

FAST

NEW YORK, Nov 19 : Alibaba was sued on Thursday in New York by shareholders who accused the Chinese e-commerce giant of defrauding them by concealing its ties to the suspected Chinese spy whose relationship with former Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang contributed to his resignation last week. According to a proposed class action filed in Manhattan federal court, Alibaba inflated its share price by knowingly and materially understating in its 2024, 2025 and 2026 annual reports the risks that actual or suspected export control violations could harm its business. Shareholders cited Alibaba's relationship with Megaspeed, a Singaporean company suspected of helping Beijing gain access to advanced Nvidia AI chips, and whose executive Alice Huang had a relationship with Jensen Huang, who is not related to her. The shareholders said Alibaba shares fell 14 per cent over four days last week because of media reports on Alibaba's ties to Alice Huang and Megaspeed, including that Alibaba had become Megaspeed's "dominant" customer.

They attributed part of the decline to a November 12 Reuters article that said Nvidia's spy scandal could spur Washington to tighten restrictions on Chinese AI companies' remote use of advanced processors. Alibaba did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Eddie Wu, its chief executive, is also a defendant. Nvidia itself faces several shareholder lawsuits over the spy scandal, including allegations of lax oversight by its directors. Wu said on Thursday that Alibaba remained on track for $100 billion in external cloud revenue and a 20 per cent EBITDA margin by 2030, despite US curbs on access to computing power that could affect the company's products and services next year. The restrictions were imposed after Huang resigned from Nvidia. In June, Alibaba sued the US government over being added to a blacklist of "Chinese military companies" that the Department of Defense linked to that country's military. Last month, a federal judge in California granted Alibaba an injunction barring the US government from denying Pentagon contracts to companies whose lobbyists also work with designated Chinese military companies. Alibaba said that restriction caused its lobbyists to retreat because they feared losing other clients, and violated its First Amendment constitutional right to speak to and petition the government. Thursday's lawsuit by Alibaba shareholder Withida Bihan seeks unspecified damages for holders of Alibaba's American depositary shares between May 23, 2024 and November 11, 2026.

US signed off on sales of nearly 900,000 AI chips to China in six months, House committee says

The US approved shipments of AI chips made by Nvidia and AMD to companies on the Pentagon's list of alleged Chinese military-backed companies.

FAST

WASHINGTON: The Trump administration approved shipments of nearly 900,000 advanced AI chips made by Nvidia and AMD for Chinese companies from December 2025 through May 2026, the House Foreign Affairs Committee said on Thursday (Nov 19). The approvals for 879,000 chip shipments by the Commerce Department included 75,000 for Alibaba, 150,000 for Tencent, 43,000 for Baidu, and 4,000 for BYD, all on the Pentagon's list of alleged Chinese military-backed companies , the committee noted. The unusual release of chip export licensing data comes as the administration of President Donald Trump faces heightened scrutiny following news about former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy , which has fueled renewed calls in Washington for a tougher stance on China. Companies had sought permission to ship over 3.4 million chips to China during the period, the documents showed. It was not immediately clear how many of the approvals resulted in actual China-bound shipments of chips, which included Nvidia's H200 and AMD's equivalent MI325X.

News surrounding Huang has turned a spotlight on instances of Nvidia AI chips being smuggled to China that went unpunished, dialing up pressure on the Trump administration to crack down on Chinese tech threats. "The fact that over 30 per cent of the AI chips sent to China were shipped to companies that the Department of War has designated as Chinese military companies is astonishing, and calls into question whether Commerce conducted any serious national security review before approving these licenses,” said Chris McGuire, a former US official and expert on the US-China technology battle. Nvidia said in a statement that the approvals were "subject to strict conditions and limited volumes." It added that "despite receiving some licenses, we have since stopped shipping H200s to China". AMD said it "complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations". Alibaba, Tencent, Baidu, BYD, the Commerce Department and the Chinese Embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Also read:

MOST DETAILED PUBLIC DISCLOSURE Former President Joe Biden had restricted Chinese access to the prized chips over fears that they would supercharge China's military and erode the US lead in artificial intelligence. But Trump in December gave the green light for Nvidia to ship its H200 chip to China, rolling back Biden-era restrictions and drawing fierce criticism from China hawks across the US political spectrum. Despite the approvals, questions swirled as to whether the AI chips were actually reaching Chinese shores. In May, Reuters reported the US had cleared about 10 companies to buy the H200, but that no deliveries had taken place. In testimony before the committee in July, Commerce Department official Jeffrey Kessler said shipments had begun but there had been 'very few'. Several major Chinese internet companies had each obtained about 10,000 H200 chips, Reuters has since reported, citing people familiar with the matter. "This is the most detailed public disclosure in the history of the Export Control Reform Act," committee Chair Brian Mast, a Republican from Florida, said upon releasing the data, referring to 2018 legislation that expanded Commerce's authority to restrict the export of sensitive technologies for national security reasons.

FAST

GUATEMALA CITY, Nov 19 : Guatemala has unveiled several expressive, life-sized stucco heads crafted in the Maya period, offering the public a look at what researchers say is a unique concentration of such sculptures from the Maya world. Dating from the seventh and eighth centuries, the pieces are part of a bigger collection unearthed at the Mirador Basin archaeological site in northern Guatemala in a series of digs over the last decade, impressing researchers with their artistry, state of preservation and the size of the collection. “There is not a single known example anywhere in the Mayan world of such a large number of sculptures recovered from a single structure,” said Douglas Mauricio, an archaeologist at the Mirador Basin Project. Major Maya cities grew in prominence beginning 3,000 years ago across a large swathe of present-day southern Mexico and several Central American nations, during a period marked by advances in mathematics, astronomy and art.

The elaborate carvings — showing expressions ranging from scrunched foreheads to broad smiles — highlight the Maya people's mastery of a wide range of artistic skills beyond the mathematics and astronomy for which they are known, said Lilian Vega de Zea, restoration director for the Mirador Basin Project. “It shows us the advanced technology they had in everything," she said. The use of colors indicated a complex process involving multiple people — some who prepared the colors, others who mixed the stucco, and a person serving as a model for the head itself, Vega de Zea said. “These heads represent important people ... they also served as a message to the society of the time, depicting someone who held a certain level of authority.” The sculptures offer clues about a later period of Maya occupation at El Mirador, when a smaller population returned to the site centuries after its Preclassic peak and maintained the earlier pieces in good condition, Mauricio said. "They continued to preserve, protect, and hold their Preclassic ancestors in high regard," Mauricio said.

Why Southeast Asia's electrification push faces a stubborn fossil fuel problem

A new global push to replace fossil fuels with electricity is gathering support at COP31, but with coal and gas still dominating Southeast Asia’s power generation, the shift could face challenges.

FAST

BANGKOK: Southeast Asia is using more electricity than ever, but much of that growth is from rising demand rather than replacing fossil fuels, highlighting the challenges facing the region as world leaders push a new global electrification target at COP31. At United Nations-led climate talks in Türkiye this week, the COP31 presidency is promoting the 35-by-35 Global Electrification Pledge, which aims to increase electricity's share of global energy consumption to 35 per cent by 2035. The pledge is designed to shift attention towards practical technologies and implementation rather than relying exclusively on emissions reduction targets. The region already gets a greater share of its energy from electricity than the global average, 25 per cent compared with 23 per cent, according to a report released this month by the International Energy Agency (IEA).

But the report found that much of that progress has come from growing electricity demand for air conditioning, appliances and industrial activity, rather than shifting away from reliance on coal, oil and gas. For Southeast Asia, where electricity demand is soaring but fossil fuels remain deeply embedded in national economies, experts say accelerating that shift will be far from straightforward. "Expanding electricity use also does not automatically translate into lower emissions unless electricity generation becomes cleaner," said Thang Nam Do, a fellow at the Australian National University's Crawford School of Public Policy. Electrification means replacing direct fossil fuel use with electricity across transport, industrial processes and buildings. It goes well beyond electric vehicles, although those are among the most visible examples. Electric technologies - such as heat pumps and electric vehicles - convert energy into useful work far more efficiently than internal combustion engines or gas boilers, which lose most of their energy as waste heat. "What sets this push apart is that it shifts the focus from simply generating clean power to fundamentally transforming how we consume energy across the entire economy," said Bruce Douglas, CEO of Global Renewables Alliance (GRA), a coalition of international renewable energy industry organisations.

Support for the voluntary electrification pledge has grown during COP31, with 75 countries and 94 organisations backing the initiative as of Wednesday (Nov 18), according to figures provided by the summit presidency.  The Philippines, Singapore and Cambodia are members of the European Commission's Electrify Now coalition, which supports efforts to accelerate the use of electricity across economies. But efforts to secure wider backing for the target have encountered resistance, with some developing countries opposing its inclusion in the summit's final declaration, according to Reuters. Vietnam has cautioned against imposing new global targets or sector-specific emissions obligations without accounting for national circumstances, although it has not explicitly rejected the voluntary COP31 pledge. The disagreement reflects the political divisions that have repeatedly hampered efforts to secure more ambitious emissions reduction commitments, particularly over how countries should share the burden of tackling climate change. Coal dependence, with the fuel accounting for almost half of regional electricity generation, grid constraints and inconsistent national policies threaten to slow progress, said GRA's regional lead for Asia-Pacific, Rexor Amancio. "I would describe Southeast Asia's progress as encouraging, but uneven, and certainly not yet at the scale required," he said. Under existing policies, Southeast Asia's electrification share could increase to 32 per cent by 2035, according to the IEA. A more ambitious scenario outlined in its report puts it at 41 per cent. That would require much faster adoption of electric technologies across transport, industry and buildings, alongside major investments in renewable energy, electricity grids and infrastructure to support growing demand. Beyond being a climate commitment, the shift to electricity has also become an economic imperative, with this year's energy crisis prompting governments to reconsider their dependence on imported fuels, said Sue-Ern Tan, head of the IEA Regional Cooperation Centre in Singapore. Around 60 per cent of Southeast Asia's crude oil imports came from the Middle East before the energy crisis, according to the IEA. The agency projects that the region's energy import bill will reach US$160 billion in 2026, adding pressure on governments to reassess their national energy strategies, technologies and international partnerships. "In particular, they're looking at ways to produce more energy domestically," Tan told CNA.

Related:

Heavily reliant on gas for decades, Thailand now finds it no longer cheap nor clean

‘Never encountered this before’: What an extreme El Nino means for Southeast Asia

FOSSIL FUELS DOMINATE Electricity demand in Southeast Asia has risen by more than 60 per cent since 2015, driven by growing industries, expanding cities and rising incomes. That is much faster than the region's overall energy consumption. But many parts of national economies remain unelectrified or fuelled by dirty energy. The transport sector is a clear example. The number of electric vehicles on the road is a visible indicator of changing technologies. Yet while EVs accounted for around 30 per cent of new car sales in Southeast Asia in the first half of 2026, electricity supplied less than 0.5 per cent of the region's transport energy needs last year, reflecting how heavily the existing vehicle fleet still relies on oil. Industrial processes fare better - at 29 per cent electrified - but many factories still burn coal and gas to produce heat, even though electric alternatives are already available, such as electric boilers and heat pumps. “It's how do we deploy that more quickly across buildings, across industry and of course across transport, where there are some easy wins that can be done,” Tan said. The IEA found that investment in switching factories to electricity has barely increased over the past decade. "Many of these challenges are as much about governance and political economy as they are about technology," said Do. Electrification can improve efficiency and reduce direct fuel consumption, but its overall emissions benefits depend on the electricity supply. If an EV is charged using electricity generated by a coal-fired power plant, for example, emissions are reduced at the vehicle's tailpipe but continue to be produced elsewhere in the energy system. The IEA reported that coal generates almost half of Southeast Asia's total electricity, while gas supplies nearly another quarter. And renewable generation would need to more than triple by 2035 to meet all additional demand in its high-electrification scenario. Dinita Setyawati, Asia strategic impact lead at Ember, an independent global energy think tank, warned that failing to expand clean power supplies could undermine the climate benefits of electrification. "Clean electrification is a critical catalyst for industrial transformation. But if electricity demand grows faster than renewable energy deployment, we risk locking ourselves into fossil fuel systems for decades to come," she said.

A vessel transporting coal on the Mahakam river in East Kalimantan, Indonesia, on August 7, 2023. (Photo: CNA/Danang Wisanggeni)

A REGION MOVING AT DIFFERENT SPEEDS Vietnam gets nearly 30 per cent of its final energy from electricity, the highest share in Southeast Asia, while Cambodia remains below 20 per cent. The contrast highlights the different challenges facing countries across the region as they seek to replace fossil fuels with electricity. It also shows there is no single path towards electrification in Southeast Asia, Do said. “More ambitious targets are technically feasible, but achieving them will depend on investment, institutional capacity and effective implementation,” he told CNA. Vietnam has emerged as the region’s largest electric car market, with nearly 180,000 sold in 2025, accounting for around 40 per cent of new car sales. But coal still generates almost half of the country's electricity, limiting the climate benefits of its growing use of electric power. Indonesia, meanwhile, has competing priorities, said Fabby Tumiwa, the CEO for the Institute for Essential Services Reform, a think tank based in Jakarta. The government is seeking to reduce its dependence on imported oil and gas by expanding the use of electricity, but its industrial development policies continue to encourage coal consumption, particularly in mineral processing and smelting. Cheap domestic coal and subsidised gas also make it harder for factories to justify switching to electricity, he said. Indonesia has made substantial progress in bringing electricity to households, but has been less successful in replacing fossil fuels across its wider economy. Coal supplied around 70 per cent of its electricity in 2025 and industrial coal consumption continues to grow And the country lacks a comprehensive national electrification strategy with sector-specific targets, despite including electrification in its broader energy plans, something that could shift if the government signs onto the COP pledge in Türkiye, Fabby said. “The technology is already there. But just through a change of policy and regulation, we can implement these kinds of electrification measures in different sectors,” he said.

Solar panels work in Quy Non, Vietnam on June 11, 2023. (AP Photo/Minh Hoang)

Elsewhere in the region, Thailand has focused on building an EV manufacturing industry, supported by government subsidies and tax incentives, while also exploring ways to replace fossil fuels in factories. Singapore has expanded EV adoption and is planning to electrify more of its port operations, although its limited renewable energy resources remain a challenge. The Philippines, meanwhile, faces high electricity costs and infrastructure constraints, with coal still generating nearly 60 per cent of its power. Regional electricity integration is essential, Tan said, highlighting renewed attention on turning the ASEAN Power Grid from a long-discussed vision into actual cross-border projects, particularly ahead of Singapore's chairmanship of the regional bloc in 2027. The grid aims to connect electricity networks across Southeast Asia, allowing countries to buy and sell power across borders, share renewable energy resources and reduce their reliance on fossil fuels. The project has made gradual progress, with nine of 18 planned cross-border electricity connections operational as of 2026. A pilot scheme already allows Laos to export electricity to Singapore through Thailand and Malaysia, while ASEAN countries signed an enhanced agreement on Nov 15 to support further regional power trading. But major investment and regulatory hurdles remain, with the IEA estimating that US$27 billion will be needed for planned cross-border connections by 2040.

“The reality is that Southeast Asia’s energy future is only stronger if we work together, and I think that has to continue to be a key ethos of this region,” Tan said.
